newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia braces for strikes as Yeltsin flies home.
newsitem.headline: Russia braces for strikes as Yeltsin flies home.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin returns to Moscow on Saturday to tackle simmering social tensions after a U.S.-Russian summit in Helsinki branded a sell-out by his communist foes.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin asked regional leaders to stay in their home towns and districts in the coming week to help keep a lid on tensions before and during a nationwide day of strikes and protests set for March 27.
Trade unions have called the day of action to protest against chronic delays in payment of wages and pensions across the vast federation.
Chernomyrdin urged regional leaders to make extra efforts to pay off wage arrears and also ordered a beefing up of security arrangements to preempt social unrest, Interfax news agency said.
"We must not allow any provocations," Chernomyrdin said.
A session of the upper house Federation Council, composed largely of regional leaders, that was planned for next week has been postponed because of the day of action, Interfax said.
Union leaders say the government and enterprises owe their workers a total of $8 billion in back pay and say they expect some seven million workers to take part in the protests.

But their plans have lost some momentum since Yeltsin, firmly back at the helm after many months of illness, ordered a radical government reshuffle that put several prominent pro-market liberals in broad control of economic policy.
One of them, first deputy premier and finance minister Anatoly Chubais, went to the mining region of Kemerovo to take part in a coal miners' union conference on Friday.
Bearing a message of goodwill from Yeltsin and about $30 million in back wages, Chubais vowed to pay all wage arrears by the end of the year and to clear the pensions backlog by June.
Miners were among Yeltsin's most loyal backers in the early 1990s but are now disenchanted with reform.
Yeltsin, who was expected to arrive back in Moscow later on Saturday, will make the final changes to the government in the coming days, Interfax said on Saturday.
Quoting Kremlin sources, it said Yevgeny Yasin, removed from his post as economy minister in the reshuffle, would be reappointed to the cabinet as minister without portfolio.
Chernomyrdin told deputies on Friday that the government changes were aimed at speeding up economic reforms.

The State Duma lower house of parliament is dominated by communists and ultranationalists who loathe Chubais for spearheading Russia's privatisation programme in the early 1990s and for his role in Yeltsin's re-election campaign last summer.
The communist opposition is also fuming over what it sees as a sell-out of Russia's national interests by Yeltsin at his Helsinki summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton on Friday.
The two presidents agreed to differ over NATO's expansion plans but vowed to press ahead with a charter defining a new relationship between Moscow and the Atlantic alliance.

Yeltsin dropped a key Russian demand that the charter should be legally binding and promised to minimise differences over NATO expansion. Moscow still opposes NATO's plans to admit members from central and eastern Europe, saying they are a threat to its own security.
The hardline communist daily Sovietskaya Rossiya called the meeting "a capitulation by the current traitorous Russian regime before the United States and NATO".
The liberal Nezavisimaya daily said Russia would start forging closer ties with Asian countries like China and India, possibly leading to the creation of a new anti-Western bloc.
The newspaper noted that Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen were both due to visit Moscow next week.
